The introduction opens with the puzzling scenario the spec names (welcome code, returned jacket, 'How much should the merchant refund?'); it is not a placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book-report opening.

'What to Take Away' does not open with 'in conclusion', is not a rephrased thesis alone or a grab bag: ¶1 synthesises, then labelled Established / Depends on context / author's synthesis lists and ten questions. ¶1 states what no section states: 'The Stacking Bug's three costs had one cause: each time, a number was computed in one place and not recorded where the next system read it', extends it to stored value, and answers so-what: 'most promotion incidents can be prevented without new software, by deciding who owns each of these records and checking that it is written.'

¶1 returns to the opening shopper: 'The chapter opened with a shopper who used a welcome code on a jacket and socks and returned the jacket. The refund is the jacket's net line price', and says it exists only if the discount was 'written to the order per line'.

The intro reader predicted the sections in order (incident, what a promotion is and touches, the five-part engine and cart-time computation, discount to invoice/refund/books with Eva's allocation and the Boomerang, stored value as ledgers, four ways and scale stages, dated examples ending with the 2027 plan, failures) and the evidence (incident, worked allocation, three platforms' documentation, accounting standards, a company filing), matching AC-4's expected; the guessed identity of the four options is a detail the introduction does not promise.

The reader computes €179.10, not €199, with €23.50 allocated in proportion (€19.90 to the jacket, €3.60 to the socks) and says the per-line net price had to be recorded on the order at placement, where the returns tool, invoice and credit note read it. Matches expected.

The reader names the unowned combination setting nobody checked against the campaign plan, and before the next campaign: one owner (with second-person approval), the campaign written with order of evaluation and stop rule, one calendar ('one owner for the combination settings, one calendar'), a staging test against every active promotion, and 'governance, not software'. Matches expected.

The reader says a gift card is value paid in advance, so a liability the merchant owes kept as a ledger, and that finance (Sanne de Wit) reconciles the platform's stored-value balances to the liability account every month. Matches expected.
